extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of the history of mathematics (advanced undergraduates, grad students, researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly account of Egyptian and early Greek geometric practice (measures, formulae, methods, and attributions to Thales and successors), discussing interpretation of ancient diagrams, empirical rules, and historical evidence. Useful for evaluating ancient procedures and the plausibility of historical mathematical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation should make formulae accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting ancient diagrams one should choose the reading (e.g. isosceles vs right-angled triangle) that makes the written rule correct or at least less inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Eisenlohr and Cantor interpret a triangle as isosceles and must assume scribal error to reconcile the area formula; other authorities take it as right-angled, in which case the rule becomes correct. The advantage of interpreting a figure so the rule is correct is emphasized as more plausible given the practical surveying skills of the people involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity conditions for trapezium area rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A trapezium area formula found in the papyri (|(a + c) x b| or similar) is only accurate under specific geometric conditions (e.g. when a non-parallel side is perpendicular to the base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes the formula is accurate only if one non-parallel side b is at right angles to the base; if the figure is merely isosceles the formula is crude and inaccurate. Assess interpretations of diagrams against these geometric validity conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edfu quadrilateral formula as approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscriptions from Edfu use a quadrilateral area formula of the form 1/4(a + c)(b + d) for sides a,b,c,d; this was used as an approximate rule for many shapes including near-rectangles and isosceles trapezia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangles are treated as quadrilaterals with one side zero; many examples are numerically given. The formula persisted long after Euclid, and should be regarded as a crude approximation rather than exact geometry; look for instances where later inscriptions omit it or replace it with more accurate methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical (practical) origin of many measurement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Many papyrus rules for areas and volumes (e.g. heap-of-corn volumes, measures involving ad hoc factors) appear to be empirical—derived from repeated practical measurement—rather than from theoretical geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Papyrus Rhind gives π ≈ 3.16; Kahun papyri give value ≈ 3.2; the procedure of finding base area then multiplying by a fixed fraction of height (not the actual height) recurs. Such discrepancies suggest measurement-based heuristics rather than geometric derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful interpretation of ancient technical terms (consistency of meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used in pyramid- and monument-problems (e.g. se-qet, ukha-thebt, pir-em-us, senti, qay en heru) must be interpreted consistently across problems; inconsistent readings can lead to contradictory geometric senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eisenlohr and Cantor assigned different senses to the same term in different problems, producing inconsistency; Borchardt showed se-qet consistently represents the cotangent of the face slope. Prefer interpretations that are uniform and that match physical measurements of monuments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical measurements to validate textual interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations of ancient geometric terms or numerical se-qet values should be checked against measured slopes and dimensions of actual monuments (pyramids, mastabas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text points out that the se-qet values from papyrus problems correspond precisely to slopes measured by Petrie and others, which supports Borchardt's uniform interpretation of se-qet as a cotangent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical implementability of proposed geometric methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When reconstructing historical procedures (e.g. Thales's methods for measuring pyramids or ship-distance), prefer methods that are simple, implementable in the field, and require minimal space or sophisticated instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simplest recorded version of Thales's pyramid measurement uses the moment when a man's shadow equals his height—requiring only observation. More elaborate constructions invoking Euclid I.26 may be harder to implement in typical field conditions; the text favors the simpler accounts as more probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation from demonstration in historical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributions such as 'demonstrated', 'stated', or 'discovered' should be treated differently: some results credited to early geometers may be mere observations rather than formal proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Thales 'demonstrated' a circle is bisected by its diameter (probably observational), 'stated' equality of base angles in isosceles triangles, and 'discovered' vertically opposite angles' equality without scientific proof. Historical evaluation must record this nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of general proof vs case-by-case verification
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical fact proved only separately for special classes (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) does not amount to knowing it 'qua triangle' unless a unified, general proof is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's point is cited: separate demonstrations for each species do not constitute a notional, general understanding. Historical credit for a theorem should consider whether a general proof was available or only case-based verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of similarity/proportionality in distance/height problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for measuring distances or heights in the ancient sources commonly rely on proportionality of similar (especially right-angled) triangles or equivalent se-qet-style calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various reconstructions of Thales's ship-distance method appeal to Euclid I.26 or practical proportional constructions; evaluate proposed historical methods on whether they directly use proportional reasoning and whether they match the likely available instruments and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simpler reconstructions when multiple historical accounts vary
rubrics_metrics.description: When sources give varying accounts (e.g. different versions of Thales's pyramid method), the simpler, earlier, or more elementary version is often the more probable historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues the earliest and simplest version (shadow-equals-height) is likely original; more general methods attributed later may be idealizations or reinterpretations. Consider chronology and practical plausibility when choosing among accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward late or single-source attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributions to early figures based on late or isolated authorities (e.g. Pamphile, Apollodorus) should be treated cautiously; such reports can conflate stories or transpose honors from later mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pamphile's claim that Thales discovered the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem is late and may reflect confusion with Pythagorean traditions. Cross-check with earlier sources and consider motives for legendary embellishment.
